result:
There is a library that has no catalog.

It exists in the junk drawer in your kitchen, in the glove compartment of your car, in the pocket of a winter coat you haven't worn since February. It is the inventory of almost-lost things.

I think about this library a lot.

In mine there is a single AAA battery, rolling loose. There is a ticket stub for a movie I don't remember seeing, but I must have seen it because I kept the stub. There are three keys and I only know what one of them opens. There is a blue IKEA pencil, worn down to a nub. A twist tie. A fortune from a fortune cookie that says "You will find what you are seeking in unexpected places," which is objectively lazy work from the fortune writer, but it has survived three moves anyway.

Everyone has one of these places. It is not quite trash, not quite treasure. It is a holding pattern for objects that have fallen out of their story.

I like to think that objects have momentum. A coffee mug has a job, a place, a narrative - it lives by the coffee maker, it goes to the sink, it goes back. But sometimes the narrative breaks. The mug goes to the bedroom and never comes back. The battery falls out of the remote and ends up under the couch. The hair tie snaps off a wrist and lives behind the washing machine for two years. These things have escaped gravity. They are in orbit.

The most interesting part is that we keep them. We don't throw away the mystery key. Even the most ruthless minimalist holds that key for a little while, jiggles it in their hand, wonders. Because to throw it away is to admit that some lock in your life will forever remain locked, or that you lost something you were supposed to protect. So it goes in the drawer. The drawer becomes a museum of minor mysteries.

Maybe that's what writing is, too. Or thinking. Or living for a while and paying attention.

We are taught that attention is about focus, about laser beams and narrowing down. But I have come to believe the opposite, that real attention is about widening. It's about letting your eye snag on the thing that is not supposed to be important.

The world is very good at telling you what is supposed to be important. Billboards, headlines, deadlines, push notifications, the person in the meeting who talks the loudest. The important things are always framed, lit, announced. It is the unannounced things that require actual seeing.

Yesterday I watched a man on the bus try to fold a paper map. It was a beautiful, doomed operation. Have you tried to fold a paper map recently? They are designed to be unfolded once and then to resist ever being flat again. It's part physics, part revenge. The man was methodical, he was humble about it, he wasn't cursing. He smoothed one corner, then the other side popped up. He flipped it over. He tried again. The people around him were looking at their phones, which contain maps that never need folding, maps that talk to you. But his map didn't talk. It just rustled. And I realized I had not heard the sound of a paper map in maybe eight years. That rustle is a specific sound - dry, larger than paper should be.

He eventually gave up, sort of, and folded it into something that was not its original shape but was compact enough to put in his back pocket. A compromise. The map agreed to be smaller if he agreed not to make it perfect.

So much of living is that negotiation.

We talk about the big events - moving, falling in love, loss, getting the job - as if those are what life is made of. And they are. But between those events there is an enormous amount of maintenance work that no one writes songs about. Dishes. Folding. Untangling cords. The act of carrying grocery bags from the car to the kitchen in one heroic, finger-cutting trip because you refuse to make two. The act of noticing that your plant is leaning hard toward the window and rotating it a quarter turn so it doesn't grow crooked.

That work is invisible when it's done right. You only notice it when it isn't done. If you don't do the dishes, you notice. If no one rotates the plant, it grows weird and then you notice. The reward for doing this work well is more work, invisibly.

I think this is why we love stories about apocalypses and leaving everything behind and starting on a desert island. Not because we want the world to end, but because we want, for five minutes, to not have to do the upkeep. To live in a world where the only task is finding water and staying alive, not remembering to buy more paper towels.

But then, even on the desert island, you would have to fold the map. You would have to make your shelter tidy. You would still have a junk drawer, only it would be a hollow in a rock where you keep the smooth stones you found that you have no use for but can't throw away.

I went for a walk this morning very early, before most people were awake. It was one of those mornings where the light is blue before it is gold. The streetlights were still on but they were irrelevant. The air had that cold, clean feeling like it hadn't been used yet. A delivery truck went by, spraying up yesterday's rain.

And for about twenty minutes, nothing happened. No profound thought, no epiphany. I just walked. I saw a cat sitting perfectly centered on a welcome mat like it owned the deed to the house. I saw a single sock on top of a mailbox, which is a mystery I choose not to solve. I saw the way the cracks in the sidewalk had been filled with tar that made black rivers. I saw a man watering his lawn in the almost-dark, and the water caught the streetlight and it looked for a second like he was throwing light.

This is what I mean about widening your attention. The world is constantly offering you these small, unsponsored moments. They don't count for anything. You can't put them on a resume. You can't even describe them later without sounding slightly insane. "I saw water look like light." But they accumulate. They become a second life, running alongside your official life.

Your official life is your inbox and your calendar and your plans and your goals. Your second life is the collection of moments when you looked up at exactly the right time and saw a flock of birds turn all at once, like a piece of cloth flipping inside out in the wind.

We need both.

For a long time I thought I needed to be more efficient, more optimized, more laser-focused. If I could just streamline my systems, I could get on top of things. If I could just find the right app, the right habit, I would finally be caught up. Now I think being caught up is not a real place. There is no caught up. There is only this week, and the strange battery in the drawer, and the negotiation with the map.

The junk drawer is not a failure of organizing. It's a very honest statement of philosophy: there are some things I do not understand yet, and I am willing to hold them for a while without needing them to be useful.

Maybe that's the most human thing we do. We hold space. For objects, for people, for ideas before we understand them. We make a little pocket of maybe.

So I am keeping the mystery keys. I am keeping the fortune. I am keeping the song that I only like the middle eight seconds of and always fast-forward to that part. I am keeping the habit of looking at the sky when I take the trash out.

Nothing important happened today. That is, nothing important that anyone else would measure. But the plant got rotated. The map got folded, badly, but folded. The cat was still on the mat. The drawer is still there, a little heavier than yesterday, holding everything that hasn't found its story yet.

And that, for today, is enough.
